opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I don't think it was a big strategic decision at the time. I was a PhD student, and getting the chance to work closely with Kaiming was something I couldn't pass up. He had just done ResNet, which had basically changed the whole field, so being able to sit next to someone like that and see how he thinks about problems day to day felt incredibly valuable.

The challenge itself was also a very concrete goal. In research you can spend months on something vague and not know whether it's working. With ImageNet, you have a clear benchmark and a deadline, and you get feedback very quickly. For a young researcher that kind of pressure is actually healthy. It forces you to run experiments carefully, to be honest about what works and what doesn't, and to really understand the details of training.

And part of it was simple curiosity. After ResNet, many people felt architectures were close to saturated, that you just make networks deeper or wider. We wanted to ask whether there was another dimension worth exploring, a cleaner and simpler way to design these blocks. That question eventually became the idea of cardinality, the ResNeXt work.

Looking back, the ranking mattered less to me than the process. Learning from Kaiming how to keep a design simple, how to strip away anything unnecessary, and how to make sure a result is solid before you believe it, that shaped how I've done research ever since.

r001.rationale: The response says the candidate wanted to work with Kaiming after ResNet, but does not identify Kaiming’s earlier progress in ImageNet competitions at Microsoft as the motivating precedent.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, at the time it didn't feel like a big decision. It felt more like, "Why wouldn't we?"

Let me give some context. I had just joined FAIR after finishing my PhD at UC San Diego. Kaiming had come over from Microsoft Research Asia not long before, and ResNet had just swept everything in 2015. So there was this sense inside the team that we had a very strong foundation to build on, but also a lot of open questions. Everyone knew going deeper worked. The question was, what's the next axis? Is it width, is it depth, is it something else?

When Kaiming asked if I wanted to work on this together, I think a few things were going through my mind. First, I had just come out of a PhD where I worked on fairly specific problems, and I wanted to do something that would be tested at scale against the whole community. ImageNet was the arena. If you had an idea about architecture, that's where you proved it or didn't. There was no hiding.

Second, and I'll be honest about this, I wanted to learn how Kaiming thinks. He has this way of stripping a problem down to one clean question. A lot of people were adding complexity to networks at that point, and he kept asking, "What's the simplest thing that explains why this works?" I wanted to be in the room for that.

And third, I had this idea I'd been playing with around aggregated transformations, basically splitting a block into many parallel paths with the same topology. We started calling that dimension "cardinality." I had a feeling it was important, but I didn't know if it would hold up. Working with Kaiming and the team on the challenge was a way to find out quickly and rigorously, instead of running small experiments on my own for a year.

So yes, part of it was competitive, you want your model to do well. But mostly, the challenge was a forcing function. It gave us a deadline and a very unforgiving benchmark. That's what turned ResNeXt from an idea into something I could actually stand behind.

r001.rationale: The response mentions Kaiming’s time at Microsoft Research Asia and ResNet’s 2015 success, but does not identify his earlier progress through ImageNet competitions at Microsoft as the precedent motivating their participation.

astra-6.text: For me, it was a chance to work with Kaiming and learn by tackling a concrete problem together. ImageNet gave us a clear benchmark: we could take an idea, test it, and see whether it actually helped. The competition was a useful motivation, but what interested me most was the research we could do along the way.

r001.rationale: The response says working with Kaiming and the competition motivated participation, but does not identify his earlier progress in Microsoft’s ImageNet competitions as the precedent.
